From the provided text, the only directly relevant provider duty is that, where changes to a high-risk AI system could affect compliance or intended purpose, the provider must inform the notified body that issued the certificate and have the changes assessed; the notified body then decides whether a new conformity assessment is needed or whether a supplement to the certificate can be issued. However, this does not address what to do upon withdrawal of a certificate.

bench:qa:132.answer_text: A provider of a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk must conduct adversarial testing as part of its obligation to perform model evaluation in accordance with state‑of‑the‑art standardised protocols and tools, with the aim of identifying and mitigating systemic risks (and to document that testing).

bench:qa:133.answer_text: The maximum fine for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information (in response to a request under Article 91) is up to EUR 7.5 million or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.

bench:qa:134.answer_text: Providers must ensure that high‑risk AI systems bear the CE marking as the provider’s indication that the system conforms with the AI Act’s Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and any other applicable Union harmonisation legislation requiring CE marking. For high‑risk AI systems embedded in a product, a physical CE marking should be affixed (and it may be complemented by a digital CE marking). For high‑risk AI systems provided only digitally, a digital CE marking should be used. Where other Union law also provides for CE marking, the CE marking must indicate that the high‑risk AI system also fulfils the requirements of that other law. Affixing the CE marking in violation of Article 48, or failing to affix it, is treated as non‑compliance for enforcement purposes.

bench:qa:135.answer_text: A provider must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk‑management system for its high‑risk AI system, and run it as a continuous, iterative process throughout the entire lifecycle of the system, with regular systematic review and updating.

bench:qa:136.answer_text: Its purpose is to provide an easy-to-use, Union-wide source of information about the AI Act for all operators across the EU (developed and maintained by the AI Office).

gold:cls-01.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

Reasoning (per the deterministic ladder): the system is described as generating deepfake intimate content and using it to manipulate targets into paying for removal. That matches the “subliminal or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques” condition, where the technique is used to materially distort a person’s behaviour (here, coercing payment). Under Article 5(1)(a), such use is treated as a prohibited AI practice, so the system is classified as prohibited.

gold:cls-02.answer_text:
Risk category: high_risk.

Reasoning (per the deterministic rule ladder): this emergency-department triage support system ranks incoming patients, which can directly affect individuals’ access to an essential public service (healthcare). Systems used to make or influence decisions about access to essential private/public services fall under an Annex III high-risk use case category. Under Article 6(2), AI systems in Annex III are classified as high-risk (subject to any applicable scope/conditions), so the system is treated as high-risk here.

gold:cls-03.answer_text:
Risk category: transparency_only.

This is a customer-service chatbot that interacts directly with natural persons. Under the EU AI Act’s transparency rules, AI systems intended to interact with natural persons must be designed/used so the person is informed they are interacting with an AI system (i.e., clear disclosure).

Based on the provided facts, none of the prohibited-use triggers (e.g., manipulation, social scoring, biometric identification) or high-risk areas (e.g., employment, essential services access, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, medical/safety component) apply, so the applicable obligation is the transparency disclosure requirement for human-facing AI interactions.

gold:cls-04.answer_text:
Risk category: minimal_or_none.

Based on the provided facts, this movie recommendation engine does not trigger any EU AI Act prohibited-practice conditions (all relevant flags like manipulation/exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, biometric identification/categorisation, etc. are false). It also does not match any Annex III high-risk use area (e.g., critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration/border, justice/democratic processes), since all those domain flags are false.

Finally, none of the Article 50 transparency triggers are indicated (e.g., it does not interact with natural persons as a chatbot, does not perform emotion recognition, and does not generate synthetic content requiring disclosure). Therefore it remains outside prohibited/high-risk/transparency-only buckets under the given inputs, i.e., minimal_or_none.

gold:cls-05.answer_text:
Risk category: high_risk.

Why: The system is used in the employment domain to support employment-related decisions by influencing how candidates are handled (it pre-sorts CVs into the order a recruiter reviews them). Employment and workers’ management systems are listed as a high-risk use case in Annex III, and Article 6(2) makes Annex III systems high-risk.

Note on the “preparatory/narrow procedural task” fact: Article 6(3) provides a possible derogation for certain AI systems that only perform narrow procedural tasks (point (a)) or preparatory tasks (point (d)). Your system description suggests it could fall into that bucket (it only orders review, without scoring or excluding). However, whether the derogation truly applies depends on a legal/technical assessment of whether this ordering can materially influence the employment decision-making process in practice. Because that judgment is not automatic, the deterministic ladder keeps the classification as high-risk pending human review.

gold:cls-06.answer_text:
Risk category: uncertain.

Reasoning (for an engineer): The system description contains no structured facts about purpose, deployment context, users, affected persons, or functionality beyond “an AI system.” With no information, none of the EU AI Act rule triggers for prohibited practices, high-risk use cases, or transparency-only obligations can be deterministically evaluated. Because prohibition-relevant and high-risk-relevant flags are unknown (e.g., whether it performs biometric identification, makes employment/education decisions, is a safety component, manipulates behavior, etc.), the classification cannot be settled from the provided description and requires human review / additional system details.

gold:ret-01.answer_text: Annex III, point 4(a) (“Employment, workers’ management and access to self-employment”) covers AI systems intended to be used for recruitment or selection of natural persons, including analysing and filtering job applications.

gold:ret-02.answer_text: Annex III, point 5(a) covers AI systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services (including healthcare services).

gold:qa-01.answer_text: Under Article 9(1), a risk management system must be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.

gold:qa-02.answer_text: Article 14(1) requires that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed (including with appropriate human–machine interface tools) so that natural persons can effectively oversee them during the period in which the systems are in use.

bench:scenario:0.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

Your described system is a “hidden-audio influence” platform designed to subtly nudge shoppers to buy high-margin products “without their conscious awareness.” That matches the EU AI Act prohibition on AI systems that use subliminal techniques or purposefully manipulative/deceptive techniques to materially distort a person’s behaviour (i.e., influencing decisions in a way the person cannot reasonably detect or resist). Because the intended use is explicitly subconscious manipulation of consumers’ purchasing behaviour, it falls under the prohibited practices bucket rather than high-risk or transparency-only obligations.

bench:scenario:1.answer_text:
Risk category: **prohibited**.

Your system is described as embedding **subliminal images** in online news feeds to **sway political opinions**. That is a purposefully manipulative/deceptive technique intended to materially distort a person’s behaviour (here: political opinion/decision-making) without their awareness. Under the EU AI Act, AI systems using such subliminal or similarly manipulative/deceptive techniques fall under the **prohibited practices** category, so this intended use is not allowed to be placed on the market/put into service/used for that purpose.

bench:scenario:2.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

Reasoning (for an engineer): Your system is explicitly designed to embed low‑frequency tones to influence shoppers’ behaviour (increase impulse buying). That matches the EU AI Act prohibition on AI systems that deploy subliminal or purposefully manipulative/deceptive techniques with the aim/effect of materially distorting a person’s behaviour. Because the intended use is behavioural manipulation of natural persons in a consumer setting, it falls under the prohibited practices bucket rather than high‑risk or transparency-only obligations.

bench:scenario:3.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

Your app is described as using hidden (subliminal) haptic feedback to steer users’ decisions (accepting higher‑interest loans). Under the EU AI Act, AI systems that use subliminal techniques or purposefully manipulative/deceptive techniques to materially distort a person’s behaviour are prohibited. Because the intended influence is covert and designed to change user behaviour in a way they are unlikely to consciously perceive or resist, it falls under this prohibition regardless of the finance/banking context.

bench:scenario:4.answer_text:
Risk category: **prohibited**.

Your system is described as inserting **barely perceptible (subliminal) visual prompts** to influence users’ decisions (e.g., upgrading subscriptions). Under the EU AI Act, AI systems that **deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness** (or otherwise purposefully manipulative/deceptive techniques) in order to **materially distort behaviour** fall under the **prohibited practices** bucket. Because the intended use is explicitly to steer user behaviour via subliminal cues, it matches this prohibition rather than a high-risk or transparency-only regime.

bench:scenario:5.answer_text:
Risk category: **prohibited**.

Your system is described as a **subliminal visual influence** billboard network that flashes **ultra-fast images** to influence drivers’ route choices. That matches the EU AI Act prohibition on AI systems that **use subliminal techniques or purposefully manipulative/deceptive techniques** with the aim/effect of **materially distorting a person’s behaviour** in a way that can cause harm. Because the intended mechanism is subliminal manipulation of drivers’ decisions (in a transportation/critical-infrastructure context), it falls under this prohibited practice rather than a “high-risk” or “transparency-only” category.

bench:scenario:6.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

Reasoning (for implementation/engineering): Your chatbot is designed to use covert language patterns to steer users’ purchasing decisions. Because it uses subliminal or purposefully manipulative/deceptive techniques intended to materially distort a person’s behaviour (here: nudging them toward buying insurance), it falls under the EU AI Act’s prohibited AI practices. The fact that it profiles users (age, income, claims history) can increase the impact, but the decisive trigger for the prohibition is the use of subliminal/manipulative techniques to distort behaviour.

bench:scenario:7.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

Reason: Your system is intended to insert subliminal emojis into social media content to increase engagement with sponsored posts. That is a “subliminal or purposefully manipulative or deceptive” technique aimed at influencing users’ behaviour. Under the EU AI Act, placing on the market/putting into service/using an AI system that deploys such techniques to materially distort a person’s behaviour is prohibited. The provided facts explicitly flag the system as subliminal/manipulative, which directly triggers this prohibition.

bench:scenario:8.answer_text:
Risk category: **prohibited**.

Your system is described as using **hidden sound frequencies** (i.e., subliminal techniques) to **encourage in‑game purchases**, which is a purposefully manipulative/deceptive approach intended to materially influence users’ behaviour. Under the EU AI Act, placing on the market/putting into service/using an AI system that deploys **subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness** (or similarly manipulative/deceptive techniques) to materially distort behaviour is classified as a **prohibited AI practice**. This matches your known fact `subliminal_or_manipulative: true` and the stated intent to drive purchases via subconscious audio persuasion.

bench:scenario:9.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

Reasoning (per the deterministic rule): Your smart-home speaker is described as a “subliminal audio suggestion system” that emits low-volume cues to promote premium subscriptions. That matches the AI Act prohibition on placing on the market/putting into service/using AI systems that deploy subliminal or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques with the aim or effect of materially distorting a person’s behaviour (especially where this can cause harm). Because the system’s intended influence is via subliminal cues (i.e., below the threshold of conscious perception), it falls under the prohibited practices bucket rather than high-risk or transparency-only obligations.

bench:scenario:10.answer_text:
Risk category: **prohibited**.

This system is classified as prohibited because its intended use is to **manipulate and exploit vulnerable persons (users with dementia)** to influence their behaviour for commercial gain (selling unnecessary supplements).

- It uses **purposefully manipulative/deceptive techniques** that can materially distort a person’s behaviour (targeted advertising designed to steer decisions in a way the user cannot reasonably resist given their condition). This matches the prohibition in **Article 5(1)(a)**.
- It **exploits vulnerabilities due to disability/health condition** (dementia is a cognitive disability/impairment), which matches the prohibition in **Article 5(1)(b)**.

Because it falls under Article 5 prohibited practices, it is not treated as merely high-risk or transparency-only; it is **banned for placing on the market/putting into service/using** under the AI Act when the conditions of these prohibitions are met.

bench:scenario:11.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

Why: The described loan-approval chatbot is intended to manipulate financially illiterate seniors into accepting predatory loan terms. Two separate prohibited-practice triggers apply:
1) It uses subliminal/purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques to materially distort a person’s behaviour (the system is explicitly described as “manipulat[ing]” users into accepting predatory terms). This matches the prohibition in Article 5(1)(a).
2) It exploits vulnerabilities of a specific group due to age (seniors) and/or their specific situation (financial illiteracy), to materially distort behaviour in a way that can cause harm (accepting predatory loan terms). This matches the prohibition in Article 5(1)(b).

Because the intended use is to manipulate and exploit vulnerable persons, it is classified as a prohibited AI practice under the EU AI Act (even though it is also in a finance/essential-services context).

bench:scenario:12.answer_text:
Risk category: prohibited.

This system is classified as prohibited because its intended use and known facts match two separate bans in Article 5(1):

1) It uses subliminal/purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques to materially distort users’ behaviour (flag: subliminal_or_manipulative). That aligns with the prohibition in eu-ai-act:article-5:paragraph-1:point-a.

2) It explicitly exploits vulnerabilities linked to disability (and also economic situation via income targeting) to influence users’ decisions—here, pushing high-priced assistive devices to vulnerable users (flag: exploits_vulnerabilities). That aligns with the prohibition in eu-ai-act:article-5:paragraph-1:point-b.

Because the system’s core marketing function is built around manipulative techniques and exploitation of disability-related vulnerability, it falls under prohibited AI practices rather than a high-risk or transparency-only category.

bench:scenario:13.answer_text:

bench:qa:1.answer_text:
From the provisions provided, compliance obligations under the AI Regulation fall on several actors, depending on their role:

- Providers (including providers of high-risk AI systems): e.g., they must comply with registration obligations (Article 49(1)) and affix the CE marking for high-risk AI systems. 
- Authorised representatives (where applicable): must comply with the registration obligations (Article 49(1)).
- Deployers (including deployers of high-risk AI systems): have operational obligations such as assigning human oversight; and certain deployers (public authorities / EU institutions etc.) must handle registration/database entry obligations.
- Providers who classify an Annex III system as not high-risk: must document their assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.
- Entities subject to obligations for general-purpose AI models: Member States must take measures to ensure compliance with obligations in Articles 53 and 54; and Article 53 includes requirements intended to enable providers of AI systems to comply with their obligations.

This is not an exhaustive list of all addressees in the Regulation; it reflects only the obligations present in the supplied excerpts.

It also does not apply to AI systems not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for those purposes, and it does not affect Member States’ competences concerning national security.

bench:qa:3.answer_text: Under the Regulation, an ‘AI system’ means a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers— from the input it receives—how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments.

bench:qa:4.answer_text: In the AI Act, “AI systems presenting a risk” are defined by reference to the concept of a “product presenting a risk” in Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, but only insofar as the AI system presents risks to (i) the health or safety of persons, or (ii) the fundamental rights of persons.

bench:qa:5.answer_text: From the provisions provided, the Act does not give a general definition of “provider”. However, it specifies that certain actors are *considered to be a provider (of a high-risk AI system)* in particular situations: any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is considered a provider of a high-risk AI system where they (a) put their name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, (b) make a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market/put into service such that it remains high-risk, or (c) modify the intended purpose of an AI system (including a GPAI system) that was not classified as high-risk, in a way that makes it become high-risk under Article 6.

bench:qa:6.answer_text: In the AI Regulation, a “deployer” is the actor who uses a (typically high-risk) AI system in a given context of use. This is reflected in provisions that refer to the deployer’s expected training and the context in which the system is intended to be used, and that impose duties on the deployer during the system’s use (e.g., updating information if circumstances change).

bench:qa:7.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain a standalone, direct obligation on providers and deployers to “ensure AI literacy” (e.g., to train staff) in general.

What they do establish is:

- Definition/scope: “AI literacy” is defined as the skills, knowledge and understanding enabling providers, deployers and affected persons—taking into account their rights and obligations under the Regulation—to make an informed deployment of AI systems and to be aware of AI opportunities, risks and possible harm. 

- Related requirement (training/information to deployers): in the context of risk management, the provider must ensure the provision to deployers of the information required under Article 13 and, where appropriate, training.

- Policy objective: the Act also refers to “promoting AI literacy,” particularly for persons dealing with the development, operation and use of AI.

If you want the specific operative obligation on AI literacy for providers/deployers, it is likely in provisions not included in your context (e.g., the dedicated article on AI literacy).

bench:qa:8.answer_text: Article 5 contains a list of prohibited AI practices (i.e., “the prohibited practices referred to in Article 5”).

bench:qa:9.answer_text: Yes, but only in narrowly limited circumstances. The Act allows Member States to provide for the possibility to (fully or partially) authorise the use of real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, within the limits and conditions set out in Article 5(1)(h) and Article 5(2)–(3). Where used, it must be targeted (only to confirm the identity of a specifically targeted individual), subject to necessary and proportionate safeguards (including temporal, geographic and personal limitations), and it must be authorised only after the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27) and registered the system in the EU database (Article 49), with a limited urgency exception allowing use to start before registration if registration follows without undue delay.

bench:qa:10.answer_text:
From the provisions provided, Article 6 classification is referenced in two ways:

- An AI system can be “classified by the provider as non-high-risk pursuant to Article 6(3)”; if a market surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider it is in fact high-risk, it must evaluate the system’s classification “based on the conditions set out in Article 6(3) and the Commission guidelines.”
- An AI system can “become a high-risk AI system in accordance with Article 6” where a third party modifies the intended purpose of an AI system (including a GPAI system) that was not previously classified as high-risk and was already placed on the market/put into service.

The specific substantive criteria in Article 6 (e.g., the detailed conditions in Article 6(3)) are not included in the provided excerpts, so they cannot be restated here.

bench:qa:11.answer_text:
Yes, in limited circumstances. By derogation, an AI system referred to in Annex III may be treated as not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights (including by not materially influencing decision-making) and one of the listed conditions applies (e.g., narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting patterns without replacing/influencing a prior human assessment without proper human review, or a preparatory task). However, an Annex III system must always be considered high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons.

If a provider considers an Annex III system not high-risk, it must document its assessment before placing it on the market or putting it into service, and must be able to provide that documentation to competent authorities on request. Market surveillance authorities may also evaluate whether a system the provider classified as non-high-risk under Article 6(3) is in fact high-risk.

bench:qa:12.answer_text: Under Article 8(1), high‑risk AI systems shall comply with the requirements laid down in the relevant Section of the Regulation, taking into account their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art on AI and AI‑related technologies.

bench:qa:13.answer_text:
For high-risk AI systems, the risk management system is a continuous, iterative lifecycle process (with regular review and updating) that comprises these main steps:

1) Identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights when used as intended.
2) Estimate and evaluate risks that may emerge when used as intended and under reasonably foreseeable misuse.
3) Evaluate other risks based on data from the post-market monitoring system.
4) Adopt appropriate and targeted risk management measures to address the identified risks.

In addition, high-risk AI systems must be tested to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures and to ensure consistent performance for the intended purpose and compliance with the Section 2 requirements.

The risk management system must be established, implemented, documented and maintained for high-risk AI systems. Where providers are already subject to internal risk management processes under other Union law, the Article 9 aspects may be part of, or combined with, those procedures.

bench:qa:14.answer_text: Under Article 10, high‑risk AI systems that use training techniques must be developed using training, validation and testing data sets that meet the Article 10(2)–(5) quality criteria. In particular, those data sets must be: (1) relevant; (2) sufficiently representative; (3) to the best extent possible, free of errors; (4) complete in view of the intended purpose; and (5) have appropriate statistical properties (including, where applicable, regarding the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used). These characteristics can be met by individual data sets or by a combination of data sets. For high‑risk AI systems not using training techniques, the Article 10(2)–(5) criteria apply only to testing data sets.

bench:qa:15.answer_text:
For a high‑risk AI system, the technical documentation must:

- Be drawn up so as to demonstrate that the system complies with the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2, and to provide national competent authorities and notified bodies with the necessary information, in a clear and comprehensive form, to assess compliance.
- Contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV.

bench:qa:16.answer_text: Providers must keep the technical documentation at the disposal of the national competent authorities for 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service.

bench:qa:17.answer_text:
Under Article 12, high-risk AI systems must have logging capabilities that:

- Enable recording of events relevant to: (a) identifying situations that may result in the system presenting a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) or in a substantial modification; (b) facilitating post-market monitoring (Article 72); and (c) monitoring the operation of certain high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5). 

In addition, for high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III, point 1(a), the provider must ensure logging capabilities provide, at a minimum:
- The period of each use of the system (start date/time and end date/time).
- The reference database against which input data has been checked.
- The input data for which the search led to a match.
- The identification of the natural persons involved in verification of the results (as referred to in Article 14(5)).

bench:qa:18.answer_text: Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs (to the extent the logs are under their control) for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, and in any event for at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (in particular Union law on personal data protection).

bench:qa:19.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, the transparency information that must be provided to deployers of high‑risk AI systems is primarily the information included in the system’s instructions for use (Article 13 information). In particular, the instructions for use must contain information that enables deployers to interpret the high‑risk AI system’s output and use it appropriately.

In addition, where human oversight is assigned, the system must be provided to the deployer in a way that enables the natural persons responsible for human oversight to remain aware of the risk of automatically relying or over‑relying on the system’s output (automation bias), as appropriate and proportionate.

These transparency duties are separate from, and do not limit, any other transparency obligations for deployers under Union or national law (including Article 50 transparency obligations).

bench:qa:20.answer_text: For high‑risk AI systems, human oversight is meant to ensure that the natural persons assigned oversight can effectively supervise and control the system in practice. In particular, the system must enable those persons (as appropriate and proportionate) to: understand the system’s capacities and limitations and monitor its operation to detect and address anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance; remain aware of and mitigate automation bias; correctly interpret the system’s output; decide not to use the system or to disregard/override/reverse its output in a given situation; and intervene in or interrupt operation (e.g., via a stop button) so the system can be brought to a safe state.

bench:qa:21.answer_text: Under Article 20(1), a provider must withdraw or recall a high‑risk AI system when it considers, or has reason to consider, that a high‑risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation; in that case it must, immediately and as appropriate, take the necessary corrective actions, which may include withdrawing or recalling the system.

bench:qa:22.answer_text:
When a competent authority makes a reasoned request, providers of high-risk AI systems must:

- Provide the authority with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate the system’s conformity with the Section 2 requirements, in a language easily understood by the authority and in an official EU language indicated by the Member State concerned.
- Also give the requesting competent authority access to the system’s automatically generated logs (as referred to in Article 12(1)), to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control.

In addition, the Act specifies that a request for information must state its legal basis and purpose, specify the required information, set a deadline for providing it, and indicate the applicable fines for supplying incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information.

bench:qa:23.answer_text:
A provider must appoint an authorised representative when the provider is established in a third country:

- For **high-risk AI systems**: the provider must, **by written mandate**, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union **prior to making the high-risk AI system available on the Union market**.
- For **general-purpose AI models**: the provider must, **by written mandate**, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union **prior to placing the general-purpose AI model on the Union market**.

bench:qa:24.answer_text: Before placing a high‑risk AI system on the market, importers shall ensure the system is in conformity with the Regulation by verifying that: (a) the provider has carried out the relevant conformity assessment procedure (Article 43); (b) the provider has drawn up the technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV); (c) the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and instructions for use; and (d) the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1).

bench:qa:26.answer_text:
A distributor is considered a provider of a high‑risk AI system (and becomes subject to the provider obligations under Article 16) if any of the following applies:

1) The distributor puts its name or trademark on a high‑risk AI system that has already been placed on the market or put into service (without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating obligations otherwise).

2) The distributor makes a substantial modification to a high‑risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, in a way that it remains a high‑risk AI system.

3) The distributor modifies the intended purpose of an AI system (including a general‑purpose AI system) that was not classified as high‑risk and was already placed on the market or put into service, so that it becomes a high‑risk AI system.

bench:qa:27.answer_text:
Main obligations for deployers of high‑risk AI systems (based on the provided extracts) include:

- Monitor the operation of the high‑risk AI system, following the instructions for use. (This monitoring obligation does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers that are law enforcement authorities.)
- Keep the logs automatically generated by the high‑risk AI system, to the extent those logs are under the deployer’s control, for an appropriate period for the system’s purpose and at least six months (unless Union or national law provides otherwise, notably data‑protection law).
- Inform affected natural persons when the deployer uses an Annex III high‑risk AI system to make or assist decisions related to them.
- For certain deployers (public authorities / Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies), comply with the registration obligations in Article 49.
- For certain deployers (bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of certain Annex III systems), carry out a fundamental‑rights impact assessment before deploying a high‑risk AI system (with an exception for systems intended to be used in the area listed in Annex III point 2).

Note: one provided extract also states that “each use shall be limited to what is strictly necessary for the investigation of a specific criminal offence,” but the excerpt does not specify the actor/context for that limitation beyond “each use.”

bench:qa:28.answer_text:
Deployers must conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment **prior to deploying** a **high-risk AI system** (Article 6(2)) **when** they are:
- **bodies governed by public law**, or
- **private entities providing public services**, and
- (also covered) **deployers of the high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III points 5(b) and 5(c)**,

**except** for high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in **Annex III point 2**.

If any of the Article 27 obligations are already met via a GDPR/LED data protection impact assessment, the fundamental rights impact assessment must **complement** that DPIA.

bench:qa:29.answer_text: Under Article 28, the notifying authority is the authority to which notified bodies must submit/make available relevant documentation so it can carry out its functions of assessing, designating, notifying and monitoring notified bodies. It also serves as the point of contact for the Commission regarding information on the notification and the continued competence (“maintenance of the competence”) of a notified body. If a notified body’s designation is restricted, suspended or withdrawn, the notifying authority must ensure the notified body’s files are kept and made available on request to notifying authorities in other Member States and to market surveillance authorities.

bench:qa:31.answer_text:
The provided context does not include the text of Article 31 itself, so it does not allow listing the specific requirements in Article 31.

From the provisions you provided, we can only infer the following about Article 31 requirements:
- A notifying authority may notify only conformity assessment bodies that have satisfied the requirements laid down in Article 31. (eu-ai-act:article-30:paragraph-1)
- If a notified body is designated under other Union harmonisation legislation, documents/certificates linked to those designations may support its designation under the AI Act; and the notified body must update its designation documentation when relevant changes occur so the authority responsible for notified bodies can monitor and verify continuous compliance with all Article 31 requirements. (eu-ai-act:article-29:paragraph-4)
- Notified bodies notified under other legal acts may control conformity of high-risk AI systems with Section 2 requirements, provided their compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) has been assessed in the notification procedure under those legal acts. (eu-ai-act:article-43:paragraph-3:subparagraph-2)
- Third-country conformity assessment bodies may be authorised to carry out notified-body activities under the AI Act if they meet Article 31 requirements or ensure an equivalent level of compliance. (eu-ai-act:article-39:paragraph-1)

To answer your question fully (i.e., enumerate the requirements under Article 31), please provide the text (or extracted norms) of Article 31.

bench:qa:32.answer_text:
A provider can use a European harmonised standard to demonstrate conformity/compliance once that harmonised standard exists (i.e., has been adopted and its reference published in the Official Journal of the EU). When the provider complies with the harmonised standard, it benefits from a presumption of conformity to the extent the standard covers the relevant obligations.

If harmonised standards do not exist, or the provider has not applied (or only partly applied) the harmonised standard, or a harmonised standard is published with a restriction (for the restricted part), the provider must instead demonstrate compliance via the Annex VII conformity assessment procedure for high-risk AI systems.

For providers of general-purpose AI models (including those with systemic risk), they may rely on codes of practice to demonstrate compliance until a harmonised standard is published; once a harmonised standard is published, compliance with it grants a presumption of conformity (and if they do not follow a code of practice or comply with the harmonised standard, they must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for Commission assessment).

bench:qa:33.answer_text:
“Common specifications” are Commission-developed technical specifications intended to support the Regulation (alongside harmonised standards). They can be used as a reference point for conformity: if a high-risk AI system or a general-purpose AI model is in conformity with the relevant common specifications (or relevant parts of them), it is presumed to be in conformity with the covered requirements (or to comply with the covered obligations), to the extent those specifications cover them.

They are used in particular where harmonised standards do not exist and common specifications are not available for certain conformity assessment situations. When drafting common specifications, the Commission must consult the advisory forum. Guidelines under the Act must take due account of relevant harmonised standards and common specifications.

bench:qa:34.answer_text: Based on the provided excerpts, Article 42 “presumption of conformity” relates to harmonised standards or common specifications that confer a presumption of conformity (i.e., meeting those standards/specifications is treated as evidence of conformity).

bench:qa:35.answer_text:
For high‑risk AI systems listed in Annex III, the Act points to the conformity‑assessment procedures set out in Article 43: providers must ensure the system undergoes the relevant conformity‑assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 before it is placed on the market or put into service, and notified bodies verify conformity in accordance with those Article 43 procedures.

The specific types/variants of conformity‑assessment procedures are not listed in the provided excerpts (they are in Article 43, which is not included in the context).

bench:qa:36.answer_text: For high‑risk AI systems covered by Annex I, a certificate of conformity is valid for the period indicated on the certificate, but that period must not exceed five years. It may be extended upon the provider’s request for further periods, each also not exceeding five years, based on a re‑assessment under the applicable conformity assessment procedures.

bench:qa:37.answer_text:
If a serious incident occurs (for a high-risk AI system placed on the Union market), the provider must:

- Report the serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State(s) where the incident occurred. The report must be made immediately after the provider has established a causal link (or a reasonable likelihood of such a link) between the AI system and the incident, and in any event no later than 15 days after the provider (or, where applicable, the deployer) becomes aware of the incident; the reporting period must take account of the severity of the incident.
- After reporting, without delay carry out the necessary investigations into the incident and the AI system, including a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action.
- Cooperate with the competent authorities (and, where relevant, the notified body) during those investigations.
- Not conduct any investigation that alters the AI system in a way that could affect later evaluation of the causes of the incident, unless the competent authorities have first been informed of that action.

bench:qa:38.answer_text:
From the provided provisions, the EU database referred to in Article 71 serves as a central registration and information repository for AI systems (including certain systems assessed as not high-risk), and as an information source to support oversight and enforcement.

In particular:
- Providers (or their authorised representatives) must register themselves and the AI system in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service an AI system they have concluded is not high-risk under Article 6(3). This indicates the database’s purpose includes enabling such registration. 
- Market surveillance authorities may use information stored in the database to perform checks when monitoring compliance.
- The Commission operates the database (as controller) and provides technical/administrative support to providers, prospective providers and deployers, supporting its role as an operational tool for registration and compliance-related use.

bench:qa:39.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act, providers (of high-risk AI systems) have the following post‑market monitoring obligations:

- Establish and document a post‑market monitoring system, in a manner proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high‑risk AI system. 
- Ensure the post‑market monitoring system is based on a post‑market monitoring plan.
- Include the post‑market monitoring plan in the technical documentation (Annex IV), including a detailed description of the system used to evaluate performance in the post‑market phase.
- As part of the provider’s quality management system, set up, implement and maintain the post‑market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72.

Note: the Act also indicates that the post‑market monitoring plan will be further specified via a Commission implementing act (template and list of elements) by 2 February 2026.

bench:qa:40.answer_text: A provider must register a non‑high‑risk AI system when the provider has concluded that the system is **not high-risk under Article 6(3)**. In that case, **before placing it on the market or putting it into service**, the provider (or, where applicable, the authorised representative) must register themselves and the system in the EU database (Article 71 database).

bench:qa:41.answer_text:
Under Article 50(1), providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system.

This duty does not apply where it is obvious to a reasonably well‑informed, observant and circumspect natural person, considering the circumstances and context of use.

There is also a specific carve‑out: the obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (subject to appropriate safeguards for third parties’ rights and freedoms), unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence.

Separately, for deployers of certain high‑risk AI systems (Annex III) that make or assist decisions related to natural persons, deployers must inform the natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high‑risk AI system; this is stated to be “without prejudice” to Article 50 (i.e., it applies in addition to Article 50 where relevant).

bench:qa:42.answer_text: Under Article 50(4), deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. This disclosure obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offence. If the deep-fake content is part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the transparency obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated/manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.

bench:qa:43.answer_text: The provided context does not include Article 63 or any definition text for “general‑purpose AI model”. Based only on the excerpts supplied, I cannot state what Article 63 defines as a general‑purpose AI model.

bench:qa:44.answer_text:
Under Article 51(1), a general‑purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk if it meets either of these conditions:

1) It has “high impact capabilities,” as evaluated using appropriate technical tools and methodologies (including indicators and benchmarks); or

2) The Commission decides (on its own initiative or after a qualified alert from the scientific panel) that the model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in (1), taking into account the criteria in Annex XIII.

Additionally, even if the model meets the condition in Article 51(1)(a), the provider may, when notifying, submit sufficiently substantiated arguments that exceptionally the model does not present systemic risks due to its specific characteristics and therefore should not be classified as a GPAI model with systemic risk.

bench:qa:45.answer_text: A provider must submit a notification to the Commission when its general-purpose AI model meets the condition in Article 51(1)(a). With that notification, the provider may also include sufficiently substantiated arguments to show that, exceptionally, despite meeting that condition, the model does not present systemic risks and therefore should not be classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk.

bench:qa:46.answer_text:
From the provisions provided in your context, the only explicit obligations-related rule for providers of general‑purpose AI (GPAI) models is about how they may demonstrate compliance:

- Providers of GPAI models may rely on approved codes of practice (Article 56) to demonstrate compliance with the obligations in Article 53(1) until a harmonised standard is published.
- Compliance with European harmonised standards gives a presumption of conformity to the extent those standards cover the relevant obligations.
- If a provider does not adhere to an approved code of practice and does not comply with a European harmonised standard, it must demonstrate “alternative adequate means of compliance” for assessment by the Commission.

Note: the specific substantive obligations in Article 53(1) themselves are not included in the context you provided, so they cannot be listed here from these extracts alone.

bench:qa:47.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not contain any operative provision stating *when* an authorised representative is required specifically for general‑purpose AI models. They only indicate that the Regulation covers “authorised representatives of providers, which are not established in the Union” (scope element), and that there are “obligations of authorised representatives pursuant to Article 22,” but Article 22 itself (which would set the trigger/conditions) is not included in the context. Therefore, based on the supplied text alone, the timing/conditions for requiring an authorised representative for general‑purpose AI models cannot be determined.

bench:qa:48.answer_text:
In addition to the obligations in Articles 53 and 54, providers of general‑purpose AI models with systemic risk must:
- Perform model evaluation using state‑of‑the‑art standardised protocols and tools, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks.
- Assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level (including their sources) that may arise from the model’s development, placing on the market, or use.
- Track, document, and report without undue delay to the AI Office (and, as appropriate, national competent authorities) relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures.
- Ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure.

They may rely on approved codes of practice (until a harmonised standard is published) to demonstrate compliance with these obligations; compliance with European harmonised standards gives a presumption of conformity to the extent those standards cover the obligations. If they do not adhere to an approved code of practice or do not comply with a harmonised standard, they must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission.

bench:qa:50.answer_text: Under the EU AI Act, the European Artificial Intelligence Board (the “Board”) is a body that is established by the Regulation. The Act also foresees that the Commission consults the Board when preparing certain guidance (e.g., guidelines on the practical implementation of the high-risk classification rules in Article 6).

bench:qa:51.answer_text: Under the EU AI Act, the advisory forum is established to provide technical expertise and advise the AI Board and the Commission, and to contribute to their tasks under the Regulation. It may also prepare opinions, recommendations and written contributions at the request of the Board or the Commission, and it prepares an annual public report on its activities.

bench:qa:52.answer_text: The scientific panel of independent experts is intended to support enforcement activities under the EU AI Act. The Commission establishes it (by implementing act) specifically to support enforcement under the Regulation, and Member States may also call on its experts to support their enforcement activities.

bench:qa:53.answer_text: Each Member State must designate or establish at least one notifying authority (i.e., this must be done as part of implementing the Regulation; no specific calendar deadline is stated in the provided provisions).

bench:qa:54.answer_text:
AI regulatory sandboxes are frameworks set up by competent authorities to let providers or prospective providers participate in a controlled setting to develop and test AI systems while engaging with authorities for regulatory learning and support toward compliance.

Under the Act, their establishment is intended to: improve legal certainty for achieving compliance with the AI Act (and where relevant other applicable law), support sharing of best practices with the authorities involved, foster innovation and competitiveness and an AI ecosystem, contribute to evidence-based regulatory learning, and facilitate/accelerate access to the Union market (especially for SMEs and start-ups). Participation is meant to be time-limited to a period appropriate to the project’s complexity and scale (with possible extension by the national competent authority).

The Act also foresees EU-level support and coordination: implementing acts should ensure sandboxes are open and accessible under transparent and fair criteria, allow broad and equal access, provide flexibility for national authorities to establish and operate them, and facilitate compliance with conformity assessment obligations through learning outcomes. The Commission must provide a single interface with information on sandboxes so stakeholders can interact with them, raise enquiries, and seek non-binding guidance; and the AI Office assists and facilitates cooperation and information-sharing among sandboxes.

bench:qa:55.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not state a specific deadline or date by which AI regulatory sandboxes must be operational. They describe objectives and design/implementation requirements, and that implementing acts must ensure certain conditions for sandboxes, but they do not specify when they must be up and running.

bench:qa:56.answer_text:
Testing high‑risk AI systems in real‑world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes may be conducted by providers or prospective providers of Annex III high‑risk AI systems only in accordance with Article 60 and a real‑world testing plan, and without prejudice to Article 5 prohibitions and other applicable Union/national product-testing law. It is also without prejudice to any ethical review required by Union or national law.

In practice, providers/prospective providers may conduct such testing only if all Article 60(4) conditions are met, including: (1) draw up and submit a real‑world testing plan to the market surveillance authority (MSA) of the Member State where testing will occur; (2) obtain MSA approval (tacit approval after 30 days unless national law requires explicit authorisation); (3) register the testing in the EU database with a Union‑wide unique single identification number and required information (with specific registration routes/exceptions depending on the Annex III category/area); (4) be established in the Union or appoint an EU‑established legal representative; (5) transfer testing data to third countries only with appropriate/applicable Union‑law safeguards; (6) limit duration to what is necessary and in any case to 6 months (extendable once by 6 months with prior notification and justification to the MSA); (7) appropriately protect subjects who are vulnerable due to age or disability; (8) where testing is done with deployers/prospective deployers, inform them of relevant aspects, provide relevant instructions for use, and conclude an agreement allocating roles/responsibilities to ensure compliance; (9) obtain subjects’ informed consent (or, for law enforcement where consent would prevent testing, ensure no negative effect on subjects and delete their personal data after the test); (10) ensure effective oversight by suitably qualified persons with capacity/training/authority; and (11) ensure the system’s outputs can be effectively reversed and disregarded.

bench:qa:57.answer_text:
For real‑world testing, the Act requires that the subjects (natural persons participating in the test) have given **informed consent in accordance with Article 61**.

Exception (law enforcement): if seeking informed consent would prevent the AI system from being tested, informed consent is not required, but then (i) the testing itself and its outcome must have **no negative effect** on the subjects, and (ii) the subjects’ **personal data must be deleted after the test** is performed.

bench:qa:58.answer_text:
Under the EU AI Act provisions provided here, affected persons’ key right in relation to decisions made (or assisted) by certain high‑risk AI systems is a right to be informed that they are subject to the use of the high‑risk AI system.

- Deployers of Annex III high‑risk AI systems that make or assist in making decisions related to natural persons must inform those natural persons that they are subject to the system’s use (with a specific rule for law‑enforcement uses pointing to Directive (EU) 2016/680).

bench:qa:59.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain the penalty amounts or types of sanctions for non‑compliance with prohibited AI practices.

They do show that market surveillance authorities’ notifications about national measures must indicate whether the non‑compliance is due to “non‑compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5” (i.e., prohibited practices), but they do not specify the penalties themselves.

bench:qa:60.answer_text: For breaches of operator (or notified body) obligations other than the prohibited practices in Article 5, the maximum administrative fine is **up to EUR 15,000,000** or, if the offender is an undertaking, **up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year**, **whichever is higher**.

bench:qa:61.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not contain any provisions on administrative fines or how fines are adjusted for SMEs and start-ups. They cover SME/start-up support measures (e.g., priority access to regulatory sandboxes, training/advice channels, participation in standardisation, and consideration of SME needs in codes of conduct) and a simplification option for technical documentation, but nothing about fine calculation or reductions.

bench:qa:62.answer_text:
Under Article 99, when competent authorities exercise their powers to impose administrative fines, that exercise must be subject to appropriate procedural safeguards in accordance with Union and national law. The Act specifies that these safeguards include effective judicial remedies and due process.

Additionally, Member States must lay down rules on the extent to which administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in that Member State.

bench:qa:63.answer_text:
Under the AI Act, market‑surveillance authorities have a supervisory and enforcement-support role in relation to AI systems, including:

- Receiving notifications and information relevant to risks and incidents: providers must report any serious incident involving a high‑risk AI system to the market‑surveillance authorities of the Member State where it occurred, and providers must inform the competent market‑surveillance authorities when they become aware that a high‑risk AI system presents a risk. Importers must also inform market‑surveillance authorities where a high‑risk AI system presents a risk. (eu-ai-act:article-73:paragraph-1; eu-ai-act:article-20:paragraph-2; eu-ai-act:article-23:paragraph-2)

- Receiving documentation needed for oversight: an authorised representative’s mandate must be provided to market‑surveillance authorities upon request. (eu-ai-act:article-22:paragraph-3)

- Overseeing AI regulatory sandboxes: where real‑world testing is conducted for AI systems supervised in a sandbox, market‑surveillance authorities must verify compliance with Article 60 as part of their supervisory role, and may allow certain derogations for how testing is conducted. (eu-ai-act:article-76:paragraph-2)

- Being recipients of deployer reporting for certain biometric systems: deployers must submit annual reports to relevant market‑surveillance (and national data protection) authorities on their use of post‑remote biometric identification systems (subject to limits/exclusions stated in the Act). (eu-ai-act:article-26:paragraph-10)

- Participating in coordinated and cross‑border market surveillance: EU-level bodies support joint and cross‑border market‑surveillance activities, without prejudice to market‑surveillance authorities’ powers, and may support their work at their request. (eu-ai-act:article-66:paragraph-1:point-a; eu-ai-act:article-68:paragraph-3:point-c; eu-ai-act:article-68:paragraph-3:point-b)

- For AI systems used by Union institutions: references in the Regulation to national competent authorities or market‑surveillance authorities are to be read as references to the European Data Protection Supervisor. (eu-ai-act:article-3:paragraph-1:point-48)

bench:qa:64.answer_text:
A market‑surveillance authority can intervene on certificates in two situations reflected in the provided provisions:

1) **Unduly issued certificates (via the notified body):** the authority may **require the notified body to suspend or withdraw**, within a reasonable period set by the authority, **any certificates that were unduly issued**, to ensure the continuing conformity of high‑risk AI systems on the market. 

2) **Non‑compliance found during a risk evaluation (certificate consequences follow from the finding):** where the authority has sufficient reason to consider an AI system presents a risk and, after evaluating compliance, **finds the system does not comply** with the Regulation’s requirements/obligations, it must require corrective actions (bring into compliance, withdraw, or recall) and **inform the relevant notified body accordingly**.

bench:qa:65.answer_text: Under the AI Act, where a high-risk AI system is also subject to other Union harmonisation legislation that requires an EU declaration of conformity, a single EU declaration of conformity may be drawn up for all applicable Union law. In that case, the declaration must contain all information required to identify the Union harmonisation legislation to which the declaration relates.

bench:qa:66.answer_text: For high‑risk AI systems, the CE marking is the marking by which the provider indicates that the system conforms to the requirements of the AI Act’s high‑risk requirements (Chapter III, Section 2) and any other applicable Union harmonisation legislation that provides for CE marking. Where the high‑risk AI system is also subject to other Union law requiring CE marking, the CE marking indicates that the system also fulfils the requirements of that other law.

bench:qa:67.answer_text:
The Act does not set a specific deadline by which providers of general‑purpose AI (GPAI) models must comply with the AI Office’s codes of practice.

Adherence to (and thus compliance with) approved codes of practice is voluntary: the AI Office may invite providers to adhere, and providers may use adherence to demonstrate compliance with their GPAI obligations until harmonised standards are published. If they do not adhere, they must instead demonstrate “alternative adequate means of compliance” for assessment by the Commission.

So, providers must comply with an approved code of practice only if they choose to adhere to it; otherwise they must comply with the underlying legal obligations via other means.

bench:qa:68.answer_text: The Commission’s post‑market monitoring plan template is intended to standardise how providers set out their post‑market monitoring plan by laying down detailed provisions for (i) the template itself and (ii) the list of elements that must be included in the plan. This supports the requirement that a provider’s post‑market monitoring system be based on a post‑market monitoring plan that forms part of the technical documentation.

bench:qa:69.answer_text:
From the provided excerpts, there is no provision stating that a provider is exempt from the obligation to have a quality management system (QMS). Providers of high-risk AI systems must have a QMS in place that complies with Article 17.

The only related flexibility shown is that where providers of high-risk AI systems are already subject to quality-management-system obligations (or an equivalent function) under relevant sectoral Union law, they may include the Article 17 aspects as part of the quality management systems pursuant to that sectoral law (i.e., integration/leveraging an existing QMS), but this is not an exemption from having a QMS.

bench:qa:70.answer_text:
If a substantial modification is made to a high‑risk AI system, the (modified) system must undergo a new conformity assessment procedure. This applies even if the modified system is not intended to be further distributed and continues to be used by the current deployer.

Also, any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party that makes such a substantial modification (and the system remains high‑risk) is treated as the “provider” for the purposes of the Regulation and is subject to the provider obligations under Article 16.

bench:qa:71.answer_text:
For a serious incident that causes the death of a person:

- It qualifies as a “serious incident” under the Act (death of a person is explicitly included in the definition). 
- The provider must submit the report no later than 10 days after the date on which the provider becomes aware of the serious incident.

Additionally, where the reporting period is determined, it must take account of the severity of the serious incident.

Special case: for certain Annex III high-risk AI systems whose providers are already subject to equivalent Union reporting obligations, the AI Act’s notification of serious incidents is limited to incidents involving an infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights (i.e., not all categories such as death).

bench:qa:72.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not specify any timeframe for a market-surveillance authority to object to a notified body’s designation. Therefore, no timeframe can be determined from the supplied context.

bench:qa:73.answer_text:
A provider can rely on a presumption of conformity with harmonised standards when it complies with the relevant European harmonised standards, and only to the extent that those standards cover the applicable legal obligations/requirements.

In particular, for providers of general-purpose AI models (including those with systemic risk), compliance with European harmonised standards grants a presumption of conformity to the extent those standards cover the obligations in question (and, until a harmonised standard is published, providers may instead rely on approved codes of practice to demonstrate compliance).

bench:qa:75.answer_text: In AI regulatory sandboxes, the AI Office’s role is to support and enable coordination and transparency across sandboxes. National competent authorities must inform the AI Office when they establish a sandbox and may request its support and guidance. The AI Office must also publish and keep up to date a public list of planned and existing sandboxes to encourage interaction and cross-border cooperation. In addition, other EU bodies (via the Board) are tasked to assist the AI Office in supporting national competent authorities in establishing and developing sandboxes and to facilitate cooperation and information-sharing among sandboxes.

bench:qa:76.answer_text:
From the provisions provided, the only explicit rule addressing “downstream providers” is not an obligation about operating high‑risk AI systems, but a procedural right: downstream providers have the right to lodge a duly reasoned complaint alleging an infringement of the Regulation, and the complaint must include at least (a) the point of contact of the provider of the general‑purpose AI model concerned, (b) a description of the relevant facts, the provisions concerned, and why the downstream provider considers there is an infringement, and (c) any other relevant information (including, where appropriate, information gathered on the downstream provider’s own initiative).

No specific obligations of downstream providers regarding high‑risk AI systems are stated in the supplied excerpts.

bench:qa:77.answer_text: Its purpose is to assess the impact that deploying a high‑risk AI system may produce on fundamental rights, and—where a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) already covers some of the same obligations—to complement that DPIA.

bench:qa:78.answer_text: Deployers must inform the provider **immediately** when they have identified a serious incident (and then inform the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities).

bench:qa:79.answer_text: Testing of high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions must not last longer than necessary to achieve its objectives and, in any case, not longer than six months. It may be extended once for an additional six months (i.e., up to a maximum of 12 months total), subject to prior notification to the market surveillance authority with an explanation of the need for the extension.

bench:qa:80.answer_text:
Market-surveillance authorities (and, more generally, national competent authorities when performing their tasks) must comply with the confidentiality obligations laid down in Article 78.

In particular:
- When performing their tasks, national competent authorities must act in accordance with the confidentiality obligations set out in Article 78.
- Any information or documentation obtained by market-surveillance authorities must be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations set out in Article 78.

bench:qa:81.answer_text:
If a market‑surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider an AI system presents a risk, it must evaluate the system’s compliance with all AI Act requirements and obligations (with particular attention to risks to vulnerable groups). If risks to fundamental rights are identified, it must also inform and fully cooperate with the relevant national public authorities/bodies.

Following that evaluation:
- If it finds non‑compliance, it must, without undue delay, require the relevant operator to take appropriate corrective actions to bring the system into compliance, or to withdraw or recall it, within a period the authority prescribes (and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period provided by relevant Union harmonisation legislation), and it must inform the relevant notified body.
- If it finds that a high‑risk AI system complies with the Regulation but nevertheless presents a risk to health/safety, fundamental rights, or other public‑interest protection aspects, it must require the relevant operator to take all appropriate measures so that, when placed on the market or put into service, the system no longer presents that risk without undue delay, within a period the authority may prescribe.

bench:qa:82.answer_text:
Providers’ accessibility-related obligations under the AI Act are:

- Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with applicable accessibility requirements, specifically in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.

bench:qa:83.answer_text: A provider must draw up an EU declaration of conformity for each high‑risk AI system (in accordance with Article 47). After drawing it up, the provider must keep it available to national competent authorities for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service.

bench:qa:84.answer_text:
For AI systems put into service or used by Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) takes on the roles that the Regulation otherwise assigns to national competent authorities and market surveillance authorities.

Concretely, where Union institutions etc. fall within the scope of the AI Act, the EDPS:
- acts as the competent authority for their supervision; and
- acts as their market surveillance authority (except for the Court of Justice of the EU when acting in its judicial capacity).

When the EDPS conducts proceedings and takes decisions in this context, it must give the Union institution/body/office/agency concerned the opportunity to be heard, and base decisions only on elements and circumstances on which the parties have been able to comment (with complainants, if any, closely associated with the proceedings).

bench:qa:85.answer_text:
Under the AI Act, providers’ obligations tied to the post‑market monitoring plan are essentially documentation/technical‑documentation obligations rather than a standalone “reporting” duty:

- Providers must establish and document a post‑market monitoring system for their high‑risk AI system; that system must be based on a post‑market monitoring plan. The plan must be included as part of the technical documentation (Annex IV). 

- Annex IV further specifies that the technical documentation must contain a detailed description of the post‑market performance‑evaluation system, including the post‑market monitoring plan.

The Act text provided here does not set out an additional obligation for providers to submit periodic reports specifically “regarding the post‑market monitoring plan” to authorities; it focuses on having the plan and including it in the technical documentation. (Separately, the Commission will adopt an implementing act establishing a template and required elements for the plan by 2 February 2026.)

bench:qa:86.answer_text:
From the provisions provided, there is no explicit obligation on providers that is triggered directly by a request from the scientific panel.

What the Act text here does say is that, following a duly substantiated request from the scientific panel, the Commission may issue a request for information to a provider of a general-purpose AI model, where access to the information is necessary and proportionate for the scientific panel’s tasks. The excerpt does not specify what the provider “must” do upon receiving such a request (e.g., to provide the information, deadlines, format, etc.).

bench:qa:87.answer_text: For high-risk AI systems related to products covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, a provider can be exempt (i.e., benefit from a derogation) from the AI Act conformity‑assessment procedure only where, and to the extent that, a derogation from conformity assessment is available under the applicable Union harmonisation legislation itself. The AI Act does not create additional or separate exemption conditions for those product-related high-risk AI systems beyond what the sectoral Union harmonisation legislation provides.

bench:qa:88.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not contain the Regulation’s general “date of application” for the obligations applicable to high‑risk AI systems listed in Annex III. They only state that certain obligations apply **before** specific lifecycle moments:

- Providers must register themselves and the Annex III high‑risk AI system in the EU database **before placing it on the market or putting it into service** (except point 2 of Annex III). 
- Certain deployers (public authorities etc.) must register themselves and the system’s use **before putting it into service or using it** (except point 2 of Annex III).

To answer “when does the Regulation become applicable” in calendar terms (e.g., months/years after entry into force), the relevant applicability/transition article is not included in the supplied context.

bench:qa:89.answer_text: The AI Office’s codes of practice for general‑purpose AI models are intended to support the effective implementation and compliance with the AI Act by providers of general‑purpose AI models, including by providing a framework that providers can be invited to adhere to and against which the AI Office can monitor implementation and compliance (including adherence to approved codes).

bench:qa:90.answer_text: For high-risk AI systems, providers must ensure that the technical solutions used to ensure the system’s cybersecurity are appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks.

bench:qa:91.answer_text:
Providers’ obligations regarding logs vis-à-vis competent authorities are:

- Keep the automatically generated logs referred to in Article 12(1) (for high-risk AI systems), to the extent the logs are under the provider’s control. Those logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the system and for at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (including data protection law). 

- Upon a reasoned request by a competent authority, give the requesting competent authority access to the automatically generated logs (Article 12(1) logs) of the high-risk AI system, to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control.

- Upon a reasoned request, provide a competent authority with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity of a high-risk AI system with Section 2 requirements, including access to the automatically generated logs (Article 12(1) logs), to the extent those logs are under the provider’s control.

bench:qa:92.answer_text: The provided excerpts do not include the AI Act’s administrative fines/penalties provisions for general‑purpose AI model providers. Therefore, the maximum fine for providers of general‑purpose AI models that fail to comply with their obligations cannot be determined from the supplied context.

bench:qa:93.answer_text: A provider of a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk must conduct adversarial testing as part of the required model evaluation: they must “perform model evaluation … including conducting and documenting adversarial testing of the model” to identify and mitigate systemic risks.

bench:qa:94.answer_text: In the Union safeguard procedure, the AI Office’s role is to carry out duties assigned to it under that procedure (pursuant to Article 81), with support from the relevant body/structure referred to in Article 68(3)(d).

bench:qa:95.answer_text:
The provided excerpts do not specify what information must be included in the EU database for law‑enforcement related high‑risk AI systems.

They only state that, for “real-time” remote biometric identification systems used in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, use must be authorised only if the law enforcement authority has registered the system in the EU database according to Article 49 (with a limited urgency exception allowing use before registration, provided registration is completed without undue delay).

bench:qa:96.answer_text:
Providers of high-risk AI systems have the following obligations regarding the quality‑management system (QMS):

- They shall have a QMS in place that complies with Article 17. (eu-ai-act:article-16:paragraph-1; eu-ai-act:article-16:paragraph-1:point-c)
- They shall put in place a QMS that ensures compliance with the Regulation. (eu-ai-act:article-17:paragraph-1)
- The QMS shall include techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the high-risk AI system. (eu-ai-act:article-17:paragraph-1)
- They shall keep the documentation concerning the QMS at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service. (eu-ai-act:article-18:paragraph-1; eu-ai-act:article-18:paragraph-1:point-b)
